analysis.one_liner: Restores FCC ownership limits and antitrust enforcement to curb radio station consolidation and radio-concert industry ties.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for the rest of the Congress and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 1996 Telecommunications Act loosened ownership rules, the bill's authors said radio station owners fell from 5,100 to 3,800 in five years, the top 50 radio groups went from owning 8.6% of stations to 27.5%, and concert ticket prices rose far faster than inflation. The bill would let the FCC revoke a station's license for repeatedly blocking independent artists and music from the air, require a hearing before any company could reach more than 60% of the national radio audience, cap local marketing deals at 35% of a market's audience or ad revenue, bar stations from loosening their own ownership caps, and prohibit stations from taking payments from record companies or concert promoters in exchange for airplay.
analysis.who_benefits: Listeners get more locally produced and independent programming; unaffiliated musicians and concert promoters get rules against being shut out of airplay or venues; concertgoers could benefit if ticket-price pressure eases; small and locally owned stations face less unfair competition from giant chains.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Listeners, independent musicians, and small stations

how_it_helps.text: Lets the FCC revoke a radio license for willful and repeated acts that significantly hinder or prevent broadcast of programming produced or promoted by people independent of the station owner [S2] [S3].

Requires a hearing before any radio applicant would exceed 60% national audience reach, and directs rules barring local marketing agreements that exceed 35% of a local market's audience share or radio advertising revenue [S2] [S3].
Freezes the FCC's existing local radio ownership limits so they cannot be raised, and removes them from the automatic biennial review required by the 1996 Act [S3].
Directs the FCC to update payola rules so a station cannot use control over what it broadcasts to extract money or other consideration from record companies, artists, or concert promoters [S2] [S3].

Bars stations from discriminating against musicians who refuse exclusive deals with affiliated concert promoters, and from improperly influencing artists' decisions to sell performances or recordings to unaffiliated venues [S2] [S3].
Requires an FCC review of whether privately controlled audience-measurement systems are being manipulated by the commercial radio industry [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large radio station groups and concert promoters that are vertically integrated with them bear the cost: harder-to-get licenses, ownership caps, a ban on extracting payments for airplay, and potential fines or license revocation for anticompetitive conduct. Radio chains argue limits like these make station investment and expansion less attractive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large radio chains and concert promoters

drawbacks.text: Making license revocation available for 'unfair or deceptive acts' that hinder independent content is a heavy sanction, and the bill limits the FCC's ability to suspend or waive its rules even for compelling cases [S3].

Enforcement is complicated: the FCC would need to determine, station by station, whether promotion practices 'improperly influence' sales of songs and concerts, with a mandated annual report to Congress on circumvention [S3].

Critics of ownership limits generally argue that deregulation following the 1996 Act helped stations invest and that ownership caps can protect unprofitable incumbents rather than listeners; the bill would freeze existing caps against any upward revision [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a documented problem: the bill's own findings cite station ownership falling 25% in five years, the top 50 groups' share of stations nearly tripling, and concert prices rising 61% from 1996 to 2001 against 13% inflation [S3]. The mechanisms — license revocation, ownership caps, payola rules — are blunt and would require careful FCC rulemaking, but the cost falls on the largest, most consolidated radio and concert interests rather than on listeners or independent artists.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Feingold introduced the bill on January 28, 2003, for himself and Senator Miller [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
The action history shows no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action after the referral for the remainder of the 108th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large consolidated radio station groups and vertically integrated concert promoters are better off: they avoided the ownership caps, payola crackdown, and license-revocation threat the bill would have imposed, without ever facing a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big radio chains and concert promoters

for.name: Russell D. Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the findings documenting radio consolidation and rising concert ticket prices.

for.name: Zell Miller and two other Democratic senators

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after referral; no action appears for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

against.name: National Association of Broadcasters
against.role: Radio and TV station trade association
against.what_they_did: The radio broadcasting industry's main lobby opposed renewed radio ownership limits of this kind during the 108th Congress, when the FCC's 2003 ownership review was a major industry priority.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee never took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill caps national audience reach at 60%, freezes local ownership limits, and lets the FCC revoke licenses for anticompetitive conduct — undoing much of what the 1996 deregulation allowed. Consolidated owners' share of stations and revenue had grown sharply under those rules [S3].

industries.industry: Concert promoters and venue owners tied to radio companies
industries.note: Vertically integrated owners could no longer use station control to steer artists to affiliated venues, require exclusive contracts, or take antitrust-violating conduct without risking license revocation. The bill's findings tie this structure to concert prices rising 61% versus 13% inflation in five years [S3].

Labels would lose the practice of paying stations or their affiliates for airplay, since the bill extends payola rules to new promotional arrangements; artists and listeners gain access to airplay that is not purchased [S3].

industries.industry: Independent musicians and locally owned stations
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is more locally and independently produced programming and protection for artists and promoters who refuse deals with affiliated companies [S3].

The FCC would have to review whether the industry manipulates privately controlled ratings systems and add measurement for rural and small markets, subjecting the firms' role in determining markets to new scrutiny [S3].
